utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Judge Nosworthy is absent for urgent personal reasons, and we have decided we ought to continue in her absence and interest of justice, so we shall do that. Your next witness, Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our next witness, Your Honour, is Djordje Curcin. He will testify under Rule 92 ter and live, and his statement is Exhibit 3D1121.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Curcin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemnly declaration to speak the truth, by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You will now be examined by Mr. Visnjic on behalf of Mr. Ojdanic. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, did you on 24 August 2007 give a statement to the investigators of the Defence team of General Ojdanic?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Upon your arrival in The Hague, did you review this statement and if you testified before a court of law would you again repeat all that?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I tender this statement as Defence Exhibit 3D1121.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I have a question concerning the statement. In paragraph 43, there's -- there's a word missing and it appears to be -- it should be the name of a person or something. It says: "While the aggression was still underway /word omitted/ personally proposed." I think we need to know that name. I don't know if it's in the original, but it's not in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, maybe we could find that out from the witness, because I believe that it is some sort of abbreviated expression.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, maybe it would be a good idea if you looked at paragraph 43 of this exhibit, 3D1121. In Serbian, it's page 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you read paragraph 43 out loud to us, please, Mr. Curcin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says: "Personally back during the aggression proposed -- and the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command accepted and ordered that the gathering of documentation drafted during the aggression be organised at all levels of command." What is missing is that I proposed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. That's now clear. Please continue, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, your statement details your military career. Is it correct that you mainly spent your career at command and operations positions?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes. Almost for 30 years I spent my military career in command and operational duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 3D690, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: While this exhibit is being prepared, General, you were retired from which position?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: From the position of the chief of the first or operations administration of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You were in that position in 1999 as well.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: When did you assume that position?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: I received that position -- I took up those duties from the 8th to the 13th January 1999, that is, the transition of duties was completed on the 13th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 3D690.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: We will soon have on the screen a directive known under the name "Grom 3" dated 16 January, 1999. I will kindly ask you to tell us first: Did you participate in the drafting of this document?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you now please look at page 5. On page 5, we see the use of the Army of Yugoslavia as it was envisaged and the assignments stipulated.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have page 5 on my screen. [In English] And both in English and Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's apparently a technical difficulty, Mr. Visnjic, about --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- Exhibiting the English, so you will have to proceed at the moment with the B/C/S alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, we see the tasks or assignments envisaged for the Army of Yugoslavia. I'm interested in para 3.1.3, that is, para 3.1, which specifies the task of the 3rd Army. Can you describe the nature of these tasks for the 3rd Army as envisaged by the plan.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes. From this description, we see the sequence and the urgency of these actions. First of all, measures to be taken for defence against attack from the air. I now see only very small lettering. So the first and the basic thing is to organise protection and defence against attack from air space. That is a defensive task. Further, to prevent the insertion of a NATO brigade from the area of Skopje, Kumanovo and Tetovo into Kosovo and Metohija, and prevent them from taking the area or installation which that brigade is supposed to take up, and then to close the possible axes of introduction of sabotage and terrorist forces from the Republic of Albania, to protect forces and installations and facilities from attacks by Siptar terrorist forces, to secure the passabilty of routes for bringing in forces from behind the lines and in coordinated action with the MUP of Serbia, blocking sabotage terrorist forces in closer areas of possible airborne assault and disable them from coordinated action with NATO forces. Those were the immediate and following tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you describe their nature.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: All of them are defensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown 3D671.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, at the collegium meeting of the 21st January 1999, a debate was conducted after which General Ojdanic asked that it be checked whether the Army of Yugoslavia had participated in the action in Racak village. Could you please look at the document before you dated the same day, 21st January 1999, and tell us more about who drafted this document and why it was drawn up.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: This is a telegram that I drafted personally on the orders of the chief of General Staff after that collegium meeting. What happened is that media carried reports about a massacre that allegedly happened in Racak in Kosovo. Several days after those first reports, the chief of General Staff ordered that it be verified. Based on his instructions and instructions from the deputy chief of General Staff, I drew up this telegram asking the commander of the 3rd Army to answer four questions and under point 5 to submit a report ASAP, that is, not later than the next morning as to what happened exactly in Racak village.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see 3D672.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, did you receive that report?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes, we received it that night, even before the deadline given, with detailed answers to the questions that we had put to the command of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: We won't go into too much detail, because the Judges can read the document, but what is the gist of this document? I believe it's in para 1.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: It was the unequivocal position of the command of the 3rd Army that the units of the Pristina Corps, as they had previously reported in their daily report, had not participated in the MUP action in Racak village.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness have in e-court 3D685.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, did we not see something the other day that indicated some involvement of the Pristina Corps with an explanation of why that was the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I remember that we discussed it and that it was mentioned during the testimony of another witness, General Obradovic, but I am not sure that these two documents were shown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We just saw the discussion that took place at the collegium meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think this will be resolved just now, but I recollect something in the last few days, I think, suggesting a reason why the VJ got drawn into the periphery of Racak, and this report would be inconsistent with that. That's the only reason I mention it. But we can have -- we'll have a look at the -- the evidence to see how the two compare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Does it mean that this is a denial of the first position, the position which was referred to just now?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is a detailed report explaining where the units of the Army of Yugoslavia were deployed, and even in the last paragraph they even list the consumption of ammunition in the area where the units were. I cannot now interpret that -- their final position, but our job is to provide you with the documents we have in relation to this event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's have this document back on the screen, please. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it was this week, the only thing that I recall, because I've been here all week, was yesterday with General Krga I directed him to a comment he made, I think, in the collegium on the 21st of January where he had said he had heard from a military attache that the VJ had been engaged or had fired in connection with Racak. But that's the only one I remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, there may have been something earlier when Mr. Stamp was here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, that may be it. But can I -- can we see this just briefly, please. Yes. Thank you, Mr. Visnjic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. So I'd asked for Exhibit 3D685. It's an evaluation of the intelligence and security situation from February 1999. Could the witness be shown page 21 in B/C/S and page 23 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, you took part in drafting this assessment, did you not?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us various scenarios were considered here what might follow after the negotiations, the scenario with the failed negotiations and the success of the negotiations and possible further developments. And one of the items was the so-called proposed measures. That was one of the headings. What would that include?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: If I were to explain to you briefly what it is, that would be the response to any challenges that might face us if the negotiations failed and if the negotiations succeed -- succeeded. At the level of the Army of Yugoslavia, the measures to be taken if the negotiations failed were all defensive in character.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: This is what we see in front of us here on the page.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes, that's item 5, "Proposed measures." Based on the entire assessment, the assessment was done in order to come up with those proposed measures. And under 5.1, we can see "Proposed measures to be taken by the VJ if negotiations fail." And then on the next page, you have 5.2 "Proposed measures to be taken if negotiations succeed." And then there is the conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I understand you correctly, those measures listed under 5.1, there is a total of 11 measures.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And these are all defensive in character.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now look at page 26 in English and page 24 in B/C/S. We can see here the signatures of the working team.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Who were members of this working team?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: The assistant chief of the Yugoslav Army General Staff for operations and staff affairs, General Obradovic; I, as the chief of the first administration; the chief of security administration, General Aleksandar Dimitrijevic; the assistant to the chief of General Staff for ground forces, General Miodrag Panic; assistant to the chief of the General Staff for logistics, General Vidoje Pantelic; the chief of the intelligence administration, General Krga; and the chief of the information and moral administration, General Gradimir Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Those are, I assume, the most important administrations in the General Staff, if I may say so.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes. As far as this task is concerned, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could we now look at Exhibit P931. This is the collegium of the 22nd of February, 1999. Could we have page 19, paragraph 5 in the English version; and in B/C/S, that would be page 17, paragraph 5. General, this is your presentation, and I'm interested in the section where you propose that the commanders of the strategic groups and the corps and the special units to -- to be ordered, to verify the readiness of their units to respond to the air raid alerts by the 6th of February and so on, and we have further tasks listed here: Planned exercise for the departure of the commands or parts of units, replenishment of units with the smokescreen-generating devices and so on. Could you just tell us briefly what is it that you are speaking of here.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: At that time, the situation was very complex, very tense, very uncertain. We, as the military, wanted to take measures to prevent surprise. We didn't want to have the situation where the NATO would launch airstrikes, and we in the commands and installations in the facilities would be caught unprepared. That is why I proposed that exercises, drills, should be carried out at all levels so that the troops could exercise leaving the facilities in a calm manner, protecting themselves, and also for creation of smokescreens using the devices that are prepared in advance in order to camouflage the disposition area, deployment area. We considered that if there would be any sudden airstrikes, the commands and institutions should be prepared for such a task lest they should sustain any casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. At the end of your presentation - that's at the next page. In English, that's page 20; and in B/C/S, that's page 18, paragraph 3 - at the very end, you make a proposal. You say: "My personal proposal is that if a Supreme Defence Council session is going to be held soon, the commanders of strategic units should attend at least a part of that session and let the comrades and gentlemen who monitor that ask themselves why the commanders are present." Could you please tell us, what does this refer to and why did you make this proposal?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes, of course I can do that. I made two proposals. This is the second one. This is my personal proposal. Because we soldiers knew best what war is all about. We expected that there would be war, and we were afraid of sudden airstrikes launched by NATO. I assessed that we were not prepared for that, that we had insufficient resources and assets and we -- and that we would sustain great casualties and that there would be a great deal of destruction in the case of such a war. What I wanted to do is to apprise the leadership, those who were most responsible, those who were making the decisions, to let them hear from the chiefs of various administrations from the strategic units what might be expected in the forthcoming period.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, thank you. And was there a meeting where the situation the army faced was presented in this manner?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes. Some ten days later a meeting was held. It was attended by the President of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Mr. Milosevic, the collegium of the chief of General Staff, and some of the commanders of strategic units. The situation was presented there and certain proposals were made.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like us to see 3D704. General, we have in front of us the aide-memoire for reporting to the President of the FRY. This is dated the 12th of February, 1999. Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes. Because the first administration participated in drafting this document, and it was submitted to the chief of General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could we please turn to page 2 of this document in B/C/S. We're still on page 1 in the English version. General, three plans were presented at this briefing -- or rather, three plans are mentioned here, but just one of them was actually presented at this briefing. Could you explain to us why and which one of those three plans was actually presented.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: The third one listed here was presented. That's Grom 3. This was the plan that was drafted in the second half of January. And it deals with the deployment of the Army of Yugoslavia in an effort to prevent the multinational NATO Brigade and its deployment in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: There's a comment here that some of the plans have already become obsolete in the time -- in just a few months.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: This is a comment made by the chief of General Staff regarding the Grom-1 plan, and in particular, Grom-2 plan, which, as indicated here, had mostly become obsolete over the past few months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is the -- the meeting you mentioned earlier with Milosevic, the collegium, and some of the commanders of the strategic units, is it? The same meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, that's the meeting on the 12th of February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Apart from Milosevic -- apart from Milosevic, was there any other civilian in attendance at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can recall, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Could the witness please be shown Exhibit P937. We need page 13 in B/C/S -- in English, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that, Mr. Curcin, can you help at all on whether the collegium has a particular definition or -- or meaning, or is it flexible or fluid organisation or body? What was its membership?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In accordance with the instruction for the internal organisation and work of the General Staff, one of the forms and methods of work is the collegium of the chief of the General Staff, comprising the chief of the General Staff with his deputy, his assistants -- or rather, sector heads, and the chiefs of independent administration. So it is quite clearly defined who the members of the collegium are. From time to time, or as needed, other persons may attend. For instance, I was not a permanent member of the collegium, but I attended all the meetings of the collegium because the first administration was indispensable for proper work. It would have been much more difficult to work without our input. You could see that we had lots of tasks. I remember that General Ojdanic had made that request at the time when he was the deputy, and General Smiljanic, my predecessor at the post of the chief of the first administration, he attended the collegium meetings. And when I took up the post, I regularly attended the meetings of the collegium.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that mean that there was a head or chief of the sector for operations and staff affairs who was a permanent member of the collegium?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there was the chief of the sector for operations and staff affairs, General Obradovic, as the chief of the sector at that time. He was succeeded by General Kovacevic. And he regularly attended the meetings. I was his deputy, and I attended the meetings regularly in order to improve the efficiency of the work and to give the General Staff a better insight into the current situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Could we please have P933, page 13 in B/C/S and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you departing from 937? Which is what I thought you asked for. Is that wrong?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. P937, page 12 on B/C/S. [Interpretation] And can we have the same document in English. And we need page 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, this is the very end of your presentation at the collegium of the 18th of February, 1999. And a very brief question regarding the three paragraphs that we see here at the beginning of the page, both in English and in B/C/S: Could you please tell me, to what do those measures refer, the measures taken in the previous -- the preceding period? We see combat readiness measures that made it possible to secure the state border, et cetera. And secondly, we have this measure regarding the mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes, the most important thing is the second item, in keeping with the increasing the threat of NATO airstrikes, mobilisation is underway of nonactive parts of units, the artillery and rocket units of the air defence and air surveillance and alerting, as well as of people possessing critical specialties and people classified as type A in air force and air defence. That would be gunners, anti-aircraft guns, radar operators, and some other operators of critical equipment. That would make it possible for us to face any sudden NATO airstrikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, could we please look at P933. That's the collegium of the 4th of March, 1999. Page 13 in the B/C/S; page 14 in English. The bottom of the page, please, in both versions. This is another presentation of yours where you proposed measures, and this is from early March 1999. With relation to your second proposed measure, what does it refer to?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: In those days, from the command of the 3rd Army and from the intelligence administration, we received verified information that the international UNPREDEP forces, which had been on the border between Yugoslavia and Macedonia, had withdrawn and been replaced by NATO forces. In our view, this indicated that something was being prepared and that there were plans to infiltrate terrorist sabotage forces from Albania through Macedonia, and that's why the command of the 3rd Army had to receive a telegram containing an order that the newly arisen situation should be assessed as regards securing the state border with Macedonia and that additional measured of the in-depth securing of the state border should be proposed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. There are some measures concerning bringing the Pristina Corps up to manpower level that are proposed here. Can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes. The first of these measures is my proposal and request that the order on bringing the Pristina Corps up to manpower level with trained soldiers from the December generation be carried out, because the chief of the General Staff in the course of 1998 issued an order that untrained soldiers could not be sent to the Pristina Corps and that they could not be trained on the territory of Kosovo. For that reason, their training was organised on the territories of the 1st and 2nd Army and also in the air force and the anti-aircraft defence. And once their training was over, several trains would be sent to the territory of Kosovo and Metohija bearing these soldiers. And this was in line with the OSCE mission. It was announced, rather, to the OSCE mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: It is stated here that some persons from the reserve forces should be released. What is this about?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Whenever the conditions were in place to downsize the army, especially the reserves, this was done. And we proposed this to the chief of the General Staff, who would then accept the proposal and order that the numbers be reduced to the necessary level. Only the necessary level.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, in the first half of 1999, there were several changes in the combat readiness measures that were in place. First of all, can you explain what combat readiness measures are. What does this mean?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Well, I can say the following: These are measures and activities undertaken in the army to ensure the necessary level of readiness of the army to respond at any moment, within 3, 6, 12, or 24 hours. These are the forces and means needed in all branches and arms of service which can eliminate unwanted situations and the time needed to prepare other forces that can be used for a certain purpose. And this was regulated in the permanent combat readiness measures, which were updated once a year. I believe that every army in the world has this but maybe under a different name.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And when you say that they have to be ready to respond at any moment within 3, 6, 12, or 24 hours, if I understand you correctly, this means that if there is a threat, an immediate threat, then the time in which the unit would have to be used is shorter.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes, the greater the threat, the greater the uncertainty. For example, airstrikes, the shorter the time. When these measures are no longer needed, then the time of combat readiness is increased. For example, from 3 hours to 6 hours and from 6 to another time period or the regular time period.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say "full combat readiness," what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Well, it may not be the best to describe it, but it means that units should be ready to respond immediately. And these are defence tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: P935, the collegium of the 11th of March, 1999, B/C/S page 11, English page 7. This is another presentation of yours and it has to do with the relocation of units in Kosovo and Metohija. And this refers to the 37th Brigade, which is being relocated and group 21 of the Nis Corps. English 11, page 11, please, paragraph 7. In this text, you say that the relocation of the 37th Motorised Brigade has been carried out from the Raska region to Kosovska Mitrovica. Can you tell us what unit this was and why it was relocated. The date is the 11th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes. This is the collegium of that date, the 11th, but I am reporting to the chief and informing the other members of the collegium, saying that the peacetime part of the 37th Motorised Brigade has been relocated from the Raska garrison to Kosovska Mitrovica. I think this was 375 or 385 men. And also, that combat group 21 from the Nis Corps has been moved to the Urosevac area and that it has been re-subordinated to the 243rd Brigade -- Motorised Brigade of the Pristina Corps. The reason was that the axis was quite open, there were no adequate forces from the Macedonian border to Kosovska Mitrovica, and there was a threat that at one point if NATO ground forces were deployed jointly with Siptar terrorist forces on that axis, the entire axis would come under threat and part of our territory would be cut off. For this reason, we carried out that task at that time and sent those two combat groups to the territory of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, this relocation, was it done in secret?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: No. No. You can't move two units of 100 or more men. This combat group 21, it had about 100 men.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: And the other one, the peacetime part of the 37th Motorised Brigade had 375 or 385 men. So it would not have been possible to take that number of men secretly to a territory covered by the OSCE mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please let's take a look at page 19 in B/C/S and page 21 in English. [No interpretation]?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We seem to have lost the interpretation, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could scroll down to the bottom of the page, please. [In English] Could we scroll down the B/C/S page. [Interpretation] And could we scroll the English version up. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Ojdanic also spoke at this collegium and informed you about talks he had had with General Clark. Can you tell us briefly how you understood General Ojdanic's presentation.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: I remember that at that point General Ojdanic commented on the situation. He mentioned the talks he had had on the 2nd with General Clark and that he informed him that he couldn't just twiddle his thumbs and keep his units in Raska while this axis was wide open and the multinational brigade forces had been increased to about 9 and a half thousand, I think, in a very brief period of time. So, of course, after this explanation as to why we had proposed and the chief of the General Staff accepted to bring that number of men, 300 to 400, to that area to avoid any surprises.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Could the witness please be shown Exhibit P1921. General, we have before us an order of the 16th of March. It was issued by the first administration. The title is "Measures for further strengthening of combat readiness order." Can you tell us what sort of document this is?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes, I can. I've already mentioned that in the preceding period at the border of Macedonia and Yugoslavia NATO had replaced the international UNPREDEP forces. For this reason and because of the increasingly complex situation and the bringing in of fresh forces on the territory of Macedonia, the chief of the General Staff ordered that the main task of the 3rd Army and the Pristina Corps had to continue to be securing the state border of Yugoslavia with Albania and Macedonia. That is the gist of this order, and it's quite clear from point 1. That's why he is giving the order that the -- that equipment, ammunitions, food and so on had to be brought in. They had to be resupplied and be prepared to carry out the task independently over a prolonged period of time, even under conditions where supplies might be cut off. And defensive measures -- other defensive measures are being ordered by the General Staff at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can we please have 3D682. This is another document issued by the General Staff, again by the first administration, signed by the chief of the General Staff, and the title is "Warning on taking measures to avoid incidents." "Warning to take measures to avoid incidents." General, under the title, where it says "warn," there are very specific warnings and orders. Could you please comment on the one under number 1.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes. Very briefly, the command of the 3rd Army is being warned to take measures of special caution immediately along the Yugoslav-Macedonian border to avoid any armed incidents and fire and provocation involving NATO forces. We were afraid that someone, whether soldiers of ours or members of the general population, perhaps in Macedonia or Siptar terrorist groups, might provoke an incident in order to create a pretext for NATO forces to act.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could we please turn to page 2 in English, and scroll the B/C/S down to the bottom of the page. I'm also interested in your comment on point 3 of the order, which says: "Movement of activity of individual, small groups and units are to be reduced to a minimum in order to avoid provocative actions by Siptar sabotage and terrorist forces which would provoke a response from our forces, which might be used as justification or cause for airstrikes."

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: It's quite clear from this that we did not want any kind of conflict. We did not want a conflict with NATO. But we did not want to provoke the sabotage terrorist forces in Kosovo and Metohija because if we were to respond and fire back, NATO might use that as cause for airstrikes. That's why he warns the command of the 3rd Army that movements of individuals, small groups and units should be reduced to a minimum to avoid any chance of provocations occurring.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, this order issued on the 20th of March, 1999, two days before that a collegium meeting was held - that was the 18th of March, 1999 - and the minutes are P938 - at which General Dimitrijevic - and we can see that on page 19 in B/C/S and page 21 in English - entered into a dialog with you; that is, General Dimitrijevic stated that certain activities of the Army of Yugoslavia are being carried out in order to provoke the KLA. And the question has arisen in the course of these proceedings as to what after these remarks by General Dimitrijevic the General Staff or General Ojdanic did. Could you please look at page 19, which is before us. Can we now turn to the next page. In both versions. Could you tell us, in fact, how this dialogue or debate between you and General Dimitrijevic ended and what the General Staff did afterwards.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: I have great respect for General Dimitrijevic. He's an experienced officer who had worked for a long time on the General Staff. But he had comments not only on my actions but many other people's. But I don't think this was a dispute. It was a discussion and the chief of General Staff asked for specific proposals. If you don't, let's move on. If people keep criticising without giving a specific suggestion what should be done instead, I don't think that's a good idea. He did not have specific proposals, though, and neither did anyone else at the collegium, but we did something after this conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What exactly?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: First of all, I held a meeting with my assistants, chiefs and officers for the 3rd Army. In my administration, we analysed the situation and I issued specific assignments as to what should be done next. And we prepared a specific order to be signed by the chief of General Staff after this discussion in my administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. Now, what -- what was his criticism, basically, General Dimitrijevic? What type of criticism he had? I mean, was it professional or was it based on any ill will or what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, I don't think there was any ill will involved. I believe that perhaps he had a different opinion at that moment or maybe he had some other information that was not available to me. So on that occasion and on a few other occasions, he presented that. But it is to be expected that before or after the meeting he could address a person -- a young person like me who was less experienced than he was, but we had known each other for 15 years and we had served on the same commands. I thought it would have been professional and friendly on his part to invite me for a coffee and tell me exactly what I could do to improve my work, rather than present it for the first time at the collegium meeting. That's what I would do for a younger colleague. That's how I would help both the colleague and the chief of the General Staff. I hope that answers your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: General Dimitrijevic is a person who has figured even earlier, because he was then -- he had to part company at some stage. Could you please tell us, what -- could you please elucidate, what was he -- what was he aiming at? I mean, what you are stating is a general statement, but can you be more specific, please, so that we understand General Dimitrijevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like you to have a better understanding of me too. I don't know exactly what he was driving at. I know what he said at the collegium meeting. It's recorded here. He disagreed with some things that I said, and the information I presented was based solely on official reports, operative reports from the subordinated commands, so that I was in no position to make things up to -- to please anyone. After this meeting, I told the officer for the 3rd Army and the officer in charge of the border belt that reports like that should always be verified so that I wouldn't be in the same position ever again. I took specific measures, and I cannot list all of them now, because we -- it would take too much time, but they did give -- yield results.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Curcin, on this page we also see reference to comments by General Pantelic about the absence of combat reports and records of the use of ammunition. That doesn't give the impression of a well-organised system of combat reporting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. I'm glad to be of assistance. In peacetime, we write operative daily reports, and only in wartime are combat reports written. General Pantelic must be confused on this point, since he's asking for combat reports. In the instructions on the work of staffs and in the rules of organisation of General Staff, no such reports are envisaged in peacetime, nor do you write about expenditure of ammunition in daily reports in peacetime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That can be listed only in combat reports and such things are mentioned under "logistical support."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So this is just drivel that we're reading in -- in this collegium minute. This is just rubbish, is it? A man that doesn't know his head from his toe.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. I -- I mean, Pantelic, according to you, is a man that just doesn't know what he's doing or what he's talking about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't say that. I said that he probably made a slip of the tongue. He wanted combat reports listing expenditure of ammunition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If he did, he made the slip of the tongue several times and he was concerned that the replenishment level for ammunition at the 3rd Army is above other units' level, which would suggest that they're using ammunition before combat operations begin. Was that a matter of concern?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe that happened too sometime, but that's not my reading of this passage and his concern. His concern was that the 3rd Army should have more ammunition than others because an aggression is expected from Albania, a ground invasion is expected, and it's natural that they should have more ammunition than units in Belgrade and -- and Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So the word "replenishment" and the other word,"resupply," don't suggest that ammunition has been used and has to be replaced. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Ammunition was probably used and a certain amount needed to be resupplied. But "resupply" does not mean that the same amount that was used needs to be replenished. Ammunition supplies have to be made in advance, because supply cannot take place when the action starts and when NATO has complete control of the air space. That, I believe, is what worried General Pantelic when he speaks about replenishment and resupply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be of assistance, Your Honour, and I can ask General Curcin directly about this contribution by General Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, this is the 18th of March. Did the Army of Yugoslavia use rockets, Plamen, Oganj, Osa, Zolja, or other rockets on the 18th of March before the airstrikes started?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: No. This is -- these are assets for anti-armour action, for combat support, and there was none of that at the time. That had to be supplied in preparation, and indeed the aggression started within seven days of this discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one final question on this. Are you saying that there was no obligation at that stage, prior to the conflict beginning, for reports to be made when -- when ammunition was used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that's not what I'm saying. It was necessary, but not on a daily basis, because our instructions did not provide for that. And as you can see in his proposal, he says: "I propose that we move on to start drafting combat reports from units of the 3rd Army that are engaged, including, of course, elements of logistical support that we would define." We used to have that earlier. We just needed to re-activate it. So automatically when something is used up during the day or during the night, it is resupplied. He is -- that's his thinking as a -- as a good logistical officer. That's his proposal. So in answer to your question, yes, there were reports made once a week, but they were drawn up technical service by technical service.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to this. You said an order was prepared, and I want to ask you now whether that is the order of the 23rd March 1999, 3D682 that I just showed you, the one that says that movements should be minimised. That's the order of the 20th of March asking that movements be minimised in order not to provoke the KLA.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes, we discussed it a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you now look at another document and tell me if some other measures were also taken trying to establish accurate information emanating from units of the 3rd Army. Could you please look at P1469. Tell me, General, what is the nature of this document? It's also from the Supreme Command Staff, 25th of March, 1999. The heading is "Accurate and verified reports, caution or warning."

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes. This is one of the first orders that came from the command post of the Supreme Command Staff. A lot of things happened in the seven days that preceded. And it underlines the need for accurate and verified reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: We can see the contents. You need not read it.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: This is only one in a series of measures emphasising the need to get accurate reports from subordinate commands. It was sent to all subordinate commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: During that war, General, were there any other orders specifying in what way and in what volume reporting should be take place?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes, there were some other orders and cautions that the system of reporting should improve.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can the witness now be shown, please, Exhibit 3D808. General, can you tell me -- this is a combat report dated the 3rd of April, 1999. Can you tell us briefly what this document is about and how it was compiled.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: The operative duty team headed by a general, and often his assistant was also a general, and there were officers from all the administrations involved, they studied the combat reports of the subordinate commands, and following certain guidelines, they compiled a combat report for the Supreme Command. Here we have certain points, certain content, and only correct and verified information received in writing from the subordinate commands were entered into this combat report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, we are especially interested in how reports from the 3rd Army, their daily combat reports, were dealt with, the ones that arrived in the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: They were all studied carefully, especially those coming from the 3rd Army, because that's where most events took place. And from these reports, most often we took the most important information if they arrived in the General Staff or at the command post in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If they arrived late, what was done with them then?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Well, they were often late due to problems in the communication system. If they were late, in order to fulfil our obligation to the Supreme Command, we would include the complete report from the 3rd Army as we had received it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now look at 3D808. That's page 3 of this document. General, we can see here that the report from the 3rd Army is attached as attachment number 1. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes. That means that the other strategic units had sent their reports on time and we processed them and the report from the 3rd Army had not arrived on time. It arrived after we've already complete our report. And that is why the full report from the 3rd Army is attached to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now could you please tell me, the text of those combat reports, they will all be exhibits in this trial, show that attachments were always provided with the combat reports. Could you please tell me briefly, what were those attachments? How many of them were there? And what did they contain?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: There would be several attachments. Because of the situation, they had to be elaborated further during the NATO airstrikes. Attachment number 1 was always an overview of the activities and situation in the 3rd Army. Attachment number 2 would always be manpower levels, replenishment, replacements, officer, non-commissioned officers, soldiers and so on. Then -- and also casualties. The next attachment was NATO airstrikes against various facilities in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia by 6.00 a.m. There was another attachment, logistics report. That was drafted by the assistant commander for logistics. And a financial report. So these would be the reports that were attached as a matter of course in most cases, and these were -- they were submitted to the general -- to the Supreme Command Staff. And I also have to note that all the requests of the subordinates are also noted here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me. Just a moment, Your Honour. I think there's a potential - at least for confusion - when the witness talks about attachments to the combat reports, I think we -- really he's talking about sections of the combat reports. This might lead you to believe when you see a combat report that there are a lot of missing attachments. And I think that's not the case. This can be confirmed with Mr. Visnjic and the witness, I think, but he -- what he just testified to is the way the combat reports are normally arranged and the paragraphs of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you help in that, Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that the witness said exactly what I wanted him to say, what I thought he should say. But let me ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, were there attachments to every combat report?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes. In addition to the paragraphs or sections in the combat report, there would always be the attachments. The attachment number 1 would be the combat report, the combat situation. The second one would be staffing levels and casualties. The third one would be the logistics, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, let me ask you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Can we see one and -- to resolve this, or are they missing, as Mr. Ackerman fears might be the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can only show what I received from the Serbian government. When I asked for combat reports, they gave me combat reports. Unfortunately, now I can -- the only thing I can do is to ask for the attachments. But sometimes the -- it is indicated in the report what the attachments are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you have a hard copy of 3D808.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do. I have it here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you give that to the witness, and we'll ask him whether the attachments are missing. Now, Mr. Curcin, you now have a copy of that combat report of the 3rd of April. Is it complete?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The report is full, but the attachments are missing. On page 4 in the Serbian version, paragraph 3.1 lists lists of casualties as -- in accordance with the attachment 2(a). On page 2, we have item 2.4, regarding the 3rd Army. We have the overview of the activities and status in the 3rd Army in accordance with the attachment number 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the attachments are not here. They're not attached to this combat report, but that's how we described things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, I think this is a suitable time for us to break, Mr. Visnjic. Mr. Curcin, we have to have a break at this stage for various reasons. That will be for 20 minutes. Could you please leave the courtroom with the usher. He'll show you where to go. And we'll see you again at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one moment with the -- the witness. The delay in returning was -- was caused by the Chamber considering the position on Radinovic, and we shall excise from the report the section on the Kosovo Liberation Army. That's Chapter 1 at 3.1. We do not think it's necessary even as background to the matters on which the expert is to report, and it would not be admissible evidence of the truth of the facts, in any event, being based on -- on remote sources when we already, of course, have evidence about the Kosovo Liberation Army and parties may yet lead more. We shall also excise the material relating to the migrations of the civilian population. That's simply a catalogue of possibilities that are matters for counsel to make submissions on based on actual evidence. So that's Chapter 2 at 5. We will not excise the parts relating to the internationalisation of the conflict, the escalation of the conflict, or the forces of the MUP, since we think all of these are necessary background. And we also think they are presented in a -- a way which is consistent with an expert's approach to matters, which is not really the situation particularly in relation to the passage on the Kosovo Liberation Army and its relationship with NATO. Now, obviously if any of the material we excise turns out to be necessary to enable the witness to express his opinions accurately, then counsel will address these in the course of his oral evidence so that any material that has to be presented from these areas which we exclude is presented in a focused and clearly relevant way. If, having digested that decision, you have any questions to clarify it, don't hesitate to ask them later in the day. We can now continue with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, while the witness is being brought in, I just want to make a correction for the transcript. Page 33, line 8, the reference should be to 3D808 and not to 3D828. The witness was shown Exhibit 3D808.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And just one thing by way of explanation, if I may. The document that was shown to the witness, I think that there was a slight confusion there among my colleagues, and I just want to clarify that now. The document was prepared by the Supreme Command Staff, and it was meant for the use of other parties. And that's the document that has attachments, not the combat report from the 3rd Army. Those combat reports from the 3rd Army do not contain any attachments. When we were talking about attachments that pertained to the reports that were put together by the Supreme Command Staff, not the reports that had come in from the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That is certainly my clear understanding, in any event. I -- I understood these were compilations from other reports submitted by --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- By individual units. And what I think you're saying is that Mr. Ackerman was referring to the individual reports that come in from which the combat report for the Supreme Command Staff is compiled.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, during the break, I reread the transcript and I was confused. And I'll chuck that up to either my age or the fact that it's Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. A combination of both, no doubt. Please continue, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, how did the reports from judicial organs come to be included in combat reports? I'm talking about the combat reports from strategic units.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question. I didn't really understand you all that well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: How did the reports from judicial organs come to be included in the combat reports of the strategic units, reports on the work of the judicial organs?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Well, as early as in late March 1999, the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command ordered that the subordinates should submit in their combat reports information about the work of the judicial organs, and they complied with this regularly. So this was part of the combat reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Could we please have Exhibit 3D688 up on the screen. General, during the war the Supreme Command Staff drafted instructions for the combat reports of the Supreme Command. So this is some kind of an internal instruction. Could you tell us something more about that?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes. The Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command was not always satisfied with the reports, and on several occasions he ordered - and this is just one such example - where he ordered in writing that an instruction be drafted as to how the reports of the Supreme Command should be drafted, because we didn't know how long the war would last, how long the aggression against our country would last. This was done so that we all deal with drafting the combat reports of the Supreme Command in the same manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: When you say "we, all of us," you mean the operations teams, the operational teams of the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I mean. I mean -- I am referring to all the organs that participated in the drafting of the combat reports. Primarily the duty operational team that was rotated every 24 hours lest every team should address this in his -- its own way.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Could we now look at page 5 in this document in both versions., B/C/S and English. General, could you please tell me, if we were now to look at the elements that are relevant for this trial in the contents of the combat report, which elements would you single out? Elements that are contained in this outline.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Although all the elements are important, I would single out item 2.8, "The situation in the territory"; 3.3, "Addressing the work of the judicial organs."

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: And paragraph 5, "Security." Of course, item number 4, "morale," it's also important. But ones that I mentioned before are particularly relevant for this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let us move on to a different topic. Could I please have 4D135 up on the screen. General, this is a document entitled "Analysis of the implementation of the requests sent by the 3rd Army to the Supreme Command Staff," issued by your sector, operations and staff affairs sector, on the 6th of June, 1999. First of all, could you tell me who was this report addressed to?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: This report was drafted in the first administration of the operations and staff affairs sector, and it was sent to the 3rd Army command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you tell me why was this analysis made?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: A few days earlier, in late May, at an evening briefing, the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command ordered that we make an analysis of all the requests that were put in from our subordinates, in particular from the 3rd Army command, and to draft a report and to prepare it for his signature and then it would be sent to the 3rd Army. That's what we did, and these are the results. If it is necessary, I can comment on it and I can say that only 2 per cent --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General. General, I have another question. When you say "we did it," did you personally take part in drafting this document?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes, I did. So did the representatives of the administration and some other administration did that and tactical mainstays dealt with the issues within their purview and we, in the first administration, put all that together and prepared the document for the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now if we can look at page 5, both in the English and the B/C/S version. I apologise. It's page 6 in the English version. General, could you please comment on the first two items -- or the first three items in this conclusion.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes. The first conclusion is that the Supreme Command Staff focused on monitoring and assessing the situation and promptly dealing with the requests made by the 3rd Army units, requests sent to the Supreme Command Staff. The second conclusion is that the request sent in by the 3rd Army command were comprehensively reviewed and assessed and they were dealt with as soon as possible by the organs of the Supreme Command Staff and that in the majority of cases those requests were approved by the Supreme Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could the witness please be shown Exhibit P1459. General, this is a document dated the 25th of May, 1999. It was sent by the 3rd Army commander to the General Staff -- or rather, the Supreme Command Staff. And now I would like you to look at page 2 of this document. I'm interested in the "Measures Proposed." The 3rd Army is requesting that the Supreme Command take certain measures within its purview. General, was this request included in the analysis that you did on the 6th of June, 1999? That's Exhibit 4D135 that you were talking about a little while earlier.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, were you aware of this document? Are you familiar with this document? I am talking now about P1459 that you have in front of you on the screen.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes, I know about this document, but that was from the proofing session before my testimony here. Anything that looked like a request and "Proposed Measures" certainly is in this category -- should have been included in our analysis of the 6th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, did you see that -- this document in 1999?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we please have document P1480. We're moving on to a different topic. General, who drafted this document? It is a memo -- or rather, a preparatory order dated the 9th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: I drafted this document and I took it up for signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us when this document was drafted and what was its purpose.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: This document was drafted on the 9th of April, 1999 on the basis of the discussion that was held the previous day, the decision was made to start drafting a directive for the defence against the aggression. It was to be distributed to the subordinate units, in particular to the 3rd Army command. This is the preparatory order. The purpose is for the army command to get ready and to make -- take measures to prepare for the aggression that may take two forms and to prepare for the briefing that was to be held the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you please comment on the variations or topics, as I would call them, that are listed here, topics that should be dealt with in the decision that was to be drafted or prepared by the 3rd Army commander.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: The most important thing was to analyse in detail and to assess in detail the possible scenarios for the aggression against our country. The first one, listed under (a), is the aggression by the Siptar terrorist forces currently in neighbouring countries, primarily in Macedonia and Albania, with the use of refugees and the support of NATO forces in collaboration with the terrorist forces in Kosovo and Metohija. So in the opinion of the Supreme Command Staff, that was the first scenario, the most probable form that the aggression would take. And the second one was the aggression by NATO forces with the activation of an armed uprising by the remaining and infiltrated Siptar terrorist forces and also making use of the refugees. The 3rd Army was to make an assessment and to prepare a directive -- or rather, to prepare its order.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And, General, did the commander of the 3rd Army report this proposal of the decision and when?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes. The commander of the 3rd Army briefed on the proposal of his decision on the 3rd of April in the staff of the Supreme Commander, where the Supreme Commander was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Let's move on. Could the witness be shown P1487. General, can you tell us -- this document has been discussed quite a lot in these proceedings. These are the so-called suggestions dated the 17th of April, 1999. What do you know about the way this document came into being?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: I know how this document came into being. One evening - and here the date is mentioned, the 17th of April - I was called up by General Ojdanic while I was at the command post, and he showed me an -- a segment of a map. The map represented the situation in the broader Rugovo area, and he asked me what I thought of it. I studied the map for two or three minutes, and at first sight, as an experienced operations officer and former commander, I gave him my opinion. I said that there was a broad basis for antiterrorist fighting, that there were no links among the units ensured, that the area was very wide, and that there were no links with the neighbouring units either, the 2nd Army and others, and that it was possible for the terrorists to pull out in -- through valleys, creeks, and so on, and I said that I doubted that an action planned in this way could be successful. It was only then that General Ojdanic told me what this was. It did say there "Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija, number 455-148 of the 15th of April, 1999 for operations in Rugova." He explained to me that several minutes before that he had met General Pavkovic who had told him he was coming from President Milosevic's office and he was carrying this map under his arm. And then it was -- it was rolled up. And after a brief conversation, he asked him what it was, and he explained that he had been to see the President and that that was the plan for the operation in the Rugovo area. He asked if he could take a look, and the other man said "yes," gave him the map and left. Immediately after that, General Ojdanic called me, and you -- you've already heard what happened. Then General Ojdanic wrote this text in his own handwriting and handed it to me to take it to the typing pool to have it typed out. I took it there. And when it was typed out, I brought it back to him. He signed it. And then I took him to the registry office at the command post to have it registered and encrypted and sent off, because it was urgent. And you can see the content for yourself. I can comment on any points, if need be.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you just tell me: If you look at the bottom part of the document, can you tell me what this stamp represents and when and where this document was sent off and to whom.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: This is an original copy. I didn't read the telegram in detail after it was typed out, which was my mistake. And when I brought it to General Ojdanic for his signature, he read it carefully and he noticed that there was a word missing in the line before last, so he personally wrote it in with a black felt-tip pen. I apologised. I wanted to take the telegram back to the typing pool to be re-typed, but he said, no, it was too urgent. The stamp shows that this was verified, that the command post - that's the one on the left; whereas, the one on the right shows when it was sent from the command post to the command of the 3rd Army. It was addressed only to the command of the 3rd Army, to the commander in person.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Could you please look at Exhibit P1746. This is a document of the sector -- operations administration. Could you please comment on this document briefly. It's dated the 20th of May, 1999, and it's from the staff of the Supreme Command, sector for operative -- operations and staff affairs.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: This was drawn up later than -- after the document we have just been talking about. The command of the 2nd Army had sent a request for joint operations -- or rather, for coordinated action - interpreter's correction - because when two units are neighbouring units and have a similar task, coordinated action is required. So he's asking for an order to be issued to the command of the 2nd and 3rd Armies to organise coordinated action. These were two neighbouring corps. And this is the gist of the telegram, and I can see that it refers to the same area. It refers to the 2nd Army and the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And in this document, as far as I can see, reference is made to the suggestions of the 17th of April, which is the document we have just seen, number P1746.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes, two documents are being referred to, and one of them is the one you've just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, to the best of your knowledge -- or rather, from what you can conclude based on these documents, is it one and the same operation or are these two separate events?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: According to what I know, it was all on the same territory, in the same area, and most probably it was the same action, because I don't remember that the first action or operation that we talked about was ever carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. There's been quite a lot of discussion here about why and whether a document should be called "Suggestion." I wish to show you 6D1130.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is an archival list. It hasn't been translated, but I only need one line from it. Could we look at page 54.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, can you read to us the text in column 112.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: "Suggestion to the command of the 3rd -- commander of the 3rd Army to take measures for the consolidation of the 7th Infantry Brigade (a total of 6 specific proposals)."

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And in column 2, also in line 112, what should be entered into that column?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what should be entered into that column, but it says "suggestion." It doesn't say "order" or "warning," it simply says "suggestion."

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Is that the column where the type of document is entered?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Whether it's an order, a warning, a brief, a report, or as it says here, "suggestion."

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And column 3?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Column 3 contains the address of the sender.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And column 4?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Column 4? The degree of confidentiality. This was a strictly confidential document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Column 5?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: 5 is the registration number from the registry book. And judging by this number, I can confirm that this is a document of the staff of the Supreme Command registered in the operations administration in our registry office. And then there follows the date, the 20th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you leave this topic, Mr. Visnjic. Mr. Curcin, the suggestions document you say was handwritten by General Ojdanic, and that would include writing on the page, the reference to the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you referring to the document we have just ... Yes. If you are asking about the document we've just looked at a little while ago, yes. The answer is "yes."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The one which followed on the delivery of the map by General Pavkovic, was there any discussion -- was there any discussion between you and -- and General Ojdanic about this expression "Joint Command"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. As we, or at least I, was focusing on the tactical situation on the map, and he told me the telegram was urgent, we did not discuss it. I was in a hurry to get the telegram typed out, signed and sent off as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've heard evidence from a very large number of generals of the Army of Yugoslavia, none of whom seems to be particularly concerned about the use of this expression in the command structure of the army. It didn't concern you at all that you were looking at a document with the words "Joint Command" on it, a body that you had never heard of before? Or perhaps I do you an injustice. Perhaps you had heard of it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps once at a collegium meeting at the beginning of the year. I had only arrived in the General Staff. I wasn't concerned about this because it was not addressed to the Joint Command. It was addressed to the commander of the 3rd Army and he was being given a precise task. So I didn't feel I ought to discuss this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In your understanding of -- of the command structure of the army, who was giving him his task?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the commander of the 3rd Army? Excuse me? It was always the chief of the staff of the Supreme Command or the President of the FRY who issued orders to the commander of the 3rd Army. To the best of my knowledge, nobody apart from those two issued orders to the commander of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who in this case was giving orders to the 3rd Army about which suggestions were being made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand your question very well. I don't know who issued the task. But I know that General Ojdanic commanded the commander of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we have, please, P1487 on the screen. You will see the reference in that document to: "Link: Kosovo and Metohija Joint Command order, number 455-148 of the 15th of April, 1999." Are we to assume that that was an order made to the commander of the 3rd Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not -- yes, but not necessarily. Let me explain. There was no text accompanying the map, so the order was not attached to the map; whereas, this text written in red felt-tip pen was written on the map itself. This may have been agreed or coordinated with the commander of the Pristina Corps or the 3rd Army somewhere. I don't know. But I just know that he brought along this map to explain it to President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So basically you did not know what was going on here. Is that your position? You didn't know who the -- who the order had been made to and you didn't know who had made the order.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.
