utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, we've just seen 6D1130. That was that table listing various documents, and one of them was entitled "Suggestion."

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Bearing in mind the contents of that document - and it refers to certain measures concerning the 7th Infantry Brigade - can you tell us, if you know, because we still don't see the document - and I hope it will be put up soon - can you tell us -- we're talking about the 25th. What could this document be about and what was the situation in the 7th Infantry Brigade at that time?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes, I know, it was a very complex situation on the ground, in some units of the Pristina Corps, and especially the 7th Infantry Brigade. The troops were scattering, deserting, carrying their weapons with them. It was a very complex situation indeed that could -- had the potential of causing problems elsewhere in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now have 3D670. General, at the beginning of the war, various interpretations circulated as to how and whether to re-subordinate the MUP to the army. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, what was the debate about? What were the dilemmas? And how was it resolved?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: More than ten days before this order was signed --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Which order?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: I'm talking about the order before me, dated the 18th April 1999. The current dilemma was whether units of the Ministry of the Interior could or could not be re-subordinated to the army. In order to solve this dilemma, communications were sent to the Ministry of Justice and Ministry of Defence, asking them to give their opinion on the issue. This procedure took several days. And I don't remember who provided this response. I think one ministry said they were not competent and the Ministry of Defence was the one that was qualified, if I understood your question correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So this is an order signed by President Milosevic on the 18th of April. Do you know anything about further orders on re-subordination?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: I know that on the basis of this document the Chief of Staff -- the Chief of Supreme Staff immediately wrote an order to subordinates. And I must say that our order was not as clear as this one. It left something to be desired. But I can say that the resulting orders of subordinated units, such as the command of the 3rd Army, that understood the superior order well and designed their own order, as did the command of the Pristina Corps. They had the best order. And I believe the Chief of the Supreme Command -- the Chief of the Supreme Command Staff said that that was a paragon, to emulate the order of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So was eventually the MUP subordinated to the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: No, that never happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the Army of Yugoslavia had ever prepared or participated in a plan to expel ethnic Albanians from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: No. No, the army never prepared any such plans. I would have had to know about that. They never prepared or trained to expel anyone, including ethnic Albanians from Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Visnjic. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General. I do have some questions for you. I would like to clear up a situation that resulted from the question of Judge Bonomy regarding document 1447. Could we call it up on the screen, P1487.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think it's 1487.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: While we are waiting for this document, General, I would like to know what General Ojdanic actually showed to you as having received from General Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: General Ojdanic showed me an excerpt of the map, a section of the map, without any text.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So when it says here "Link: Kosovo and Metohija Joint Command order, strictly confidential," et cetera, et cetera, have you ever seen this?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What about General Ojdanic?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't think so. Because it was not attached to these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So let us conclude. All that you and General Ojdanic had in your hands when General Ojdanic wrote in hand the text of a future telegram was this section of a map.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you tell us where the order number was derived from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It was written in black pen on the map: "Decision for operation. Order of the Joint Command," with a number. It was some sort of heading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So far I've had the impression there was no text at all. You said "a section of the map without any text." It now appears that there was text. Could you make sure you've told us everything about what was written on the map before any more questions are asked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was, conditionally speaking, the title of the map. In the left-hand top corner, there was no signature of approval. In the bottom corner, there was no signature or stamp of the person who made the map. Except the lines in red and blue depicting our forces and terrorist groups in the area, they -- there were only the names of units in black pen. There was no accompanying text, no accompanying table, and there was no order, just the title of the map. And the map was not verified. It was obviously some sort of working material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was the title of the map, then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot recall exactly the word order, but it was "Decision for operation." And below that: "Order of the Joint Command." And as it says here: "strictly confidential," number such-and-such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And are you saying that as far as you're aware, without having the order, General Ojdanic was able to think up and write down suggestions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. I could have done that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: General, in order to specify, to define how a proper map should look - you were in that chain of command - what is the proper appearance of a map that a commander provides together with an order? What are the necessary components of a map that was done legitimately according to military regulations?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: First of all, in the left top corner there should be an indication of the rank and title of the person approving the decision. In the left bottom corner, there should be the full name, rank, and the position of the person who made the map, together with a stamp over that signature. Once the decision is approved, in the spot below the signature of the approving officer a stamp should be affixed. Those are the basic parameters that make the map legitimate and according to our rules. In addition, there should be a legend, a key explaining the signs used. Although, on this map there were very few tactical signs. Everything was quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All the components that you just enumerated, were they there on that map that General Ojdanic showed you?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Therefore, what could you conclude about the validity of that document from the viewpoint of the military doctrine prevailing in the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: My conclusion then and now is that it was some sort of background material, working map that helped explain a certain situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: General, sir, as Judge Bonomy said, we have heard a great number of generals here, and they all spoke about the chain of command in the Army of Yugoslavia in 1998 and 1999. Could you tell us, was the chain of command in the army intact and how did it work? What was the principle of command in our army?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: The chain was intact. At the level of the Supreme Command Staff or the General Staff, it was the chief of the General Staff that issued orders to commanders of armies. Commanders of armies issued orders to corps commanders. Corps commanders issued orders to brigade commanders, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You started the chain of command with the chief of General Staff. Later it was the chief of the Supreme Command Staff. But who gave him his orders?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: He received his orders from the President of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Since you were present at all collegium meetings during the war - I'm now talking only about the war - do you know in which way those orders were passed by President Milosevic on to General Ojdanic? Was it in direct contact? Was it verbal? Written?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: I recall only this one written order that we've just seen. I don't know if there were any others. But we received no other written order in the operations administration. They were in daily contact. They met the -- the chief of the General Staff reported to the President every day and received his assignments. We learned about it every day, particularly at evening briefings, through the assignments that we received.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Perhaps you know, but perhaps you don't, that I represented Mr. Sainovic. In one part of the indictment, it says that Slobodan Milosevic conveyed his suggestions to General Ojdanic through Mr. Sainovic during the war, and it was in this way that he exercised his power over the army. What would you say about this claim?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: It makes no sense. There's no logic to it. And that's not the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: General, thank you. To conclude with this document before you, both the map and this document and what General Ojdanic dictated into it, is it a military operation or some sort of mixed operation? Is there a mention of any civilians or the MUP?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: This is a purely military operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have completed my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Curcin, let me have something clarified from what I asked you earlier. You said that you would be able to write these suggestions without knowing what was in the order, on the basis of the map and nothing else. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Absolutely. Maybe not in so many words, but that's the gist. That's the essence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Look at paragraph 3 of the suggestions which are still on the screen.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How would you have been able to determine how long to delay?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: I've already said that there was quite a lot of space between units. They had to come closer to each other. That's a very rugged, very difficult terrain in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Curcin, before you can make a suggestion about delay, you have to know what date is envisaged for implementation of the order. How did you know or how would you know that it wasn't already ordered for implementation on the 19th of April?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: I can only infer that in their discussions they reached the conclusion that the readiness is the next day, on the 18th in the morning. And from everything that happened later, in view of this telegram -- do you want me to continue or shall I stop here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, you're now indicating -- you're now indicating that to make that suggestion, you have have to have more information. You would have to know what the original plan was.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: There are two possibilities: One is that it was written on the map "readiness," such-and-such hour, such-and-such a day. That's a real possibility. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry. You don't know whether it was written on the map.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Another possibility is that General Pavkovic told him verbally when he was giving him the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, could you look at paragraph 2, please, which says that the main objective should be destruction. How would you know to make that suggestion?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: The objective of all our operations against the terrorists was to destroy them; in particular, given the ruggedness of the terrain, it was impossible to have as our objective to block them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just --

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: -- Or anything of that, so sort, but just to inflict casualties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just stop there. Why on earth then would it be put in as a suggestion if that was the objective of every operation?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Well, we have several items among the suggestions. First of all, that preparations should continue; secondly, that deficiencies in the tactical disposition should be corrected and that gaps should be closed between units. And that is why in paragraph 3 it is suggested that the task be delayed and that coordination be set up with the 3rd Army, which had not been the case before, so there would be no blocking and destruction unless there were coordination with the 2nd Army. And that was what I myself understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one final question on this. It -- how often have you seen suggestions documents? You've -- your attention has been drawn to one from the archive. Were they a frequent occurrence in the command structure?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: No, this did not happen often. I don't recall seeing any other such documents, but that was up to the commander to decide whether he would write an order, a warning, information, or a suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- I'm not able to determine right now if I have cross-examination for this witness until I have a chance to consult with my client. I suggest that I do that at the normal break and defer my cross until I'm able to do that, rather than interrupt the proceedings. But I have some notes from him that I need to discuss with him before I make that determination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. We shall proceed with any other cross-examination. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I am not opposed to Mr. Ackerman's suggestion. I have just one very brief question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Curcin, good day. My name is Mihajlo Bakrac. I'm one of the lawyers representing General Lazarevic. I have just one question for you. You -- in your examination-in-chief, you speak about the reinforcements for the 3rd Army and the Pristina Corps. You spoke about the 37th Motorised Brigade or elements from the 37th Motorised Brigade and the Nis Corps group 21. Could we please have on our screens document 5D248. And I would just like to ask you whether the plan order -- or rather, the directive Grom-3 - and I assume that this was also present in the previous directive during the tenure of General Perisic - that it was anticipated that the 3rd Army should be reinforced with the combat group 3 and combat group 252 from the 252nd Armoured Brigade.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes, the Grom-3 directive and the previous directives envisaged that the Pristina Corps or the 3rd Army should be reinforced, as indicated here, by combat group 3 from 63rd parachute Brigade. A combat group from the 37th Brigade, and a combat group from the 252nd Brigade, which was part of the 1st Army. The overall strength was about 300 people. And we have the exact figure in this overview, which is 309.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Thank you very much. I hope that I really was very brief and that I didn't tax you too much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... As you know, I am one of the attorneys for General Lukic. I will just briefly have some questions for you. You have testified regarding Exhibit 3D670, the order for re-subordination of the MUP by President Milosevic. Now, I'd like to clear up something. At paragraph 36 of your statement you say that: "The VJ General Staff did not have effective control of the MUP. It did not forward orders to the MUP. It did not even -- it did not receive reports and there was no exchange of representatives." Now, the question I have for you, General, is: Do you mean to say that the staff of the Supreme Command did not send any order or communication to Minister Stojiljkovic [Realtime transcript read in error "Stojkovic"] of the Serbian MUP as foreseen by directive 2 of 3D670, President Milosevic's directive on re-subordination?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: I saw this order by President Milosevic, and it came to my administration, this order regarding the re-subordination of the MUP forces to the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: My question, sir, is: When you say that the General Staff of the VJ did not send any orders to the MUP, are you confirming that the staff of the High Command, the staff of the Supreme Command, did not send this order or any order meant to effectuate this order of President Milosevic to Minister Stojiljkovic or any other superior official within the Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: The General Staff or, rather, the Supreme Command Staff did not send this or any other to Minister Stojiljkovic, not Stojkovic. So no orders were sent. He was not part of our chain of command, and it was impossible. There was no need for us to send any orders to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, we have heard evidence here that the MUP of Montenegro officially sent a -- officially refused to implement re-subordination. Do you have personal knowledge of any written act or communication sent by Minister Stojiljkovic of the Serbian MUP or any other high official of the Serbian MUP to the staff of the Supreme Command refusing to implement re-subordination?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: No. The Supreme Command Staff did not receive any written order from Minister Stojiljkovic or from any high-ranking official of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I apologise. I was waiting for the transcript to catch up with us. Just a few more questions. Now, in your statement and in your testimony, you have referenced your familiarity with the combat reports, the "borbena izvestaja", of all VJ units during the war. Am I correct that not a single combat report ever reported of problems undertaking any combat action arising out of any refusal of the MUP to obey or undertake VJ orders for that operation?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down for interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And am I correct -- or strike that. Tell me if this is correct, General: As I understand it, the Law of Defence and President Milosevic's order relates only to subordination for combat activities, actions, "borbane dejstva." It does not re-subordinate Minister Stojiljkovic to the Army of Yugoslavia, nor does it subordinate the assistant ministers and the remainder of the MUP to the staff of the Supreme Command. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Thank you for your time. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: General, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Hannis. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I would like to wait for Mr. Ackerman to make his decision before I begin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does it really matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It does mo me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are there areas you cannot explore that don't concern him?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, there are areas --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you interested in one principal area?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I am interested in a number of areas, Your Honour. However, I don't know how many of those will overlap over with Mr. Ackerman or if any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Curcin, we have to have another break now for about half an hour. If you could again please leave the courtroom with the usher, and we will resume at twenty minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you have questions, Mr. Ackerman? Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: General Curcin, I want to show you a document. It's P1725, and it will be up on your screen pretty soon. You'll recall speaking earlier about the the -- the study of requests from the 3rd Army and what was done with them. And I want to show you this request from the 3rd Army and ask you if you saw it; and if you did, was it dealt with in your report on dealing with 3rd Army requests?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: May I see the whole document, the second page included.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: And the third, if there is a third page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... You can read the entire document, because I think it's important that you do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Judge, I have a hard copy, if that will help the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sure it would, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You recall seeing that before?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: No. In the proofing session for my testimony, I saw this document, this telegram. It is unsigned. It does not bear a stamp. There is not the log indication, and there is no indication that it was ever received at the Supreme Command. And we can see that it was actually addressed to the sector for the ground forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What is the stamp in the upper right-hand corner on the first page?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: The stamp just below the indication "Keep permanently" is probably from the archive of the Yugoslav Army, but it's not all that legible, so I can't be completely certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Maybe if we can blow it up a little bit, maybe you can see it better. It clearly says "Vojska Jugoslavija" on it.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes, we can see that it says here: "Military archives, Belgrade."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So the document was in the archives, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Probably, given that it bears the stamp of the military archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And General Krga told us yesterday that it was in the archives, that means that it's genuine. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Well, I was in the archive. I don't know what importance can we attach to the fact that General Krga was in the archives and confirmed this was authentic. It is apparent that this document was certified by a stamp of the military archives. That's on page 1 of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There was a translation error and you didn't get the question that I asked. You got something else. The question that I asked was this: General Krga told us yesterday that if a document had an archive stamp like this on it, that meant that it was an authentic document. You agree with General Krga in that regard?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: In principle, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, you'll notice in the first paragraph of that document it first talks about an SVK team. What would that be?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Well, that would be the Supreme Command Staff and the team that had analysed the situation in the Pristina Corps a few days before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you'll notice that he refers to a document of the SVK of 29 May 1999, doesn't he?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then what he says in paragraph 1, numbered "1", is that one of the things that was brought out by that visit from the Supreme Command was that the MUP forces are not re-subordinated to appropriate VJ commands because they did not receive orders from their superior commands. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was anything done at the General Staff level to solve this problem either as pointed out by General Pavkovic in this communication or as pointed out by the team that conducted this visit?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes, the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command discussed this with President Milosevic, even before this telegram and probably after this telegram.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, a discussion with Milosevic doesn't solve the problem. What was done to solve the problem? Was anything done to solve the problem?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: I know that things were done, but now as to whether the problem was solved or -- or not, I think it is quite clear that the MUP was never re-subordinated to the army, which means that it wasn't solved, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. That's all I have. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, have you some estimate of how long you might be?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- I had estimated that I would -- yesterday I told Mr. Visnjic I would probably be about two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think that's still correct or maybe a little more, because there were some things that came up in cross-examination by other individuals as well as questions asked by the Court. You asked some of the questions I would have asked, but some of those answers you got raised additional questions. So I -- I think I'm still at that two-hour time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We would be able to -- at least two of us would be able to sit a little longer, but not long enough to solve -- we can't obtain the necessary court time to sit long enough to complete it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So it looks as though you'll just need to do what you can. And if that's the case, there's no point in us going beyond 1.45 today.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So I think you should proceed on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will. I appreciate that, Your Honour. I would try to go faster if I thought we could get him done, but I appreciate -- I appreciate that. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General. You told us -- you told Mr. Visnjic with regard to the 16 January 1999 directive that referred to Grom-3 that it set out the specific task for the 3rd Army. And you mentioned that by looking at the sequence and the urgency of these actions, you could -- well, you described the nature of these tasks based on sequence and the urgency. I have a question for you about: What was the urgency those tasks related to potential NATO bombing on the 16th of January? I mean, you -- the October agreements had been reached. This is even before the Rambouillet negotiations. What was so urgent in the middle of January?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: First of all, good afternoon to you too. I don't recall whether I actually spoke about urgency or importance, but I was referring to the importance and, hence, the urgency of events, because on the basis of that element, you assigned them their position in the sequence of the tasks in the directive. So it's the importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this -- this plan was -- it was a contingency plan; correct? It was what you were going to do if certain other events took place first. If NATO did something, then this is what you were going to do to counter it. Right? This is not an operational plan. This is a contingency plan.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: I don't know the difference between the operational plan and the contingency plan. I don't know what you mean by that. But in any case, if somebody wants to bring in thousands of troops into our territory by force, that is an emergency situation and we had to prepare for that. There were about two and a half thousand troops there at one point. This figure increased. There was this danger that they might move into our territory without our approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand. And maybe it's a matter of -- of language.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Zecevic on his feet, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, I believe the witness said 9.500 people, not 2.500.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that would be consistent with previous answers, yes. Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I think that there may be a language problem. I'm talking about a contingency plan as being something that you are preparing for a situation that may arise in the future. And what I referred to as an operational plan would be where you are directing troops to do something in terms of going to locations and taking actions. And this Grom-3 on the 16th of January is called a directive. Now, if the troops had been ordered to go such -- such-and-such a location and set up a blockade at such-and-such a time, I would expect to see a document entitled "Order." Am I correct about that distinction between a directive and an order?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: There is a huge difference between a directive and an order, but I'm not sure whether you are doing it properly. An order is for a specific action in a specific area. A directive is a much more complex document. It deals with a situation in a much more complex manner and it deals with a longer period of time, several week, several months.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But an order usually has a starting time, such as a certain date and a certain hour; and a directive, from what I've seen, has -- has a provisional time. It doesn't have a date and an hour, but it's connected to or triggered by some future event, which may or may not take place. Is that a fair distinction?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked about the -- the Racak event and what the Supreme Command did to check into what had happened. You -- we saw the -- the document that you drafted requesting information from the 3rd Army and the response you got back. Your answer today at page 6 was that it was the unequivocal position of the command of the 3rd Army that the units of the Pristina Corps had not participated in the MUP action in Racak. Now, let me ask you this question, because we have had some evidence that some of the -- one or more of the international observers believed that the VJ was supporting that MUP operation in Racak and had observed fire by, I think, tanks. I note in the Exhibit 3D672, which is the 3rd Army's response to you, that, I think, six 100-millimetre tank shells were used, 30 -- 30 anti-aircraft rounds, and ten 120 mortar shells. Now, if that ammunition had been fired by VJ units in the nearby vicinity, is it possible that the international observers may have viewed that as VJ supporting the MUP operation in Racak by firing on KLA who might try to come to the support of their colleagues, neighbours, family, friends in Racak village proper?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question, because there were so many other things. What do you want me to tell you, in briefest possible terms? Whether the observers were right or something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, whether -- whether they could have reached that conclusion, whether it was right or wrong, that seeing tanks in the nearby vicinity firing in the general direction of Racak or at neighbouring villages where there were believed to be other KLA forces could that have been interpreted by the international observers as VJ acting in support of the MUP operation that was going on in Racak the same day.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes, the army had its presence in the vicinity. And if you look at the telegrams closely - and I was interrupted, so I couldn't complete it - 3rd Army units from the combat group that was in the vicinity came under an attack and fire was opened from anti-armour rockets were launched at them, anti-aircraft guns and rifles. And they organised themselves and they opened fire on those attacking them on the hills around this area and Ranci [phoen]. And it is quite specifically noted here that they did not open fire on the inhabited area, the area of Racak. And if the objection OSCE observers interpreted that as support, yes, you could interpret it that way but only as indirect support because fire was opened outside of the Racak sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand. Thank you. I want to go now to the 2nd of February. There was a VJ collegium meeting on that day. And this is from Exhibit P931. And I think you told us that the VJ collegium wanted to apprise the state leadership, the ones who were making the decisions, about what you thought the situation was and what the strategic units might be doing in the forthcoming period. You told us that the -- some ten days later there was a meeting held attended by President Milosevic. And the document we talked about in conjunction with that was 3D704. If we could put that up on the screen for you, General. Actually, I -- I have a hard copy here. I can hand that to you. That may make it easier. Thank you. And I understand that is an aide-memoire, I guess, prepared to insist General Ojdanic in presenting the points to the President. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you yourself attend this meeting?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Were there any minutes or any kind of record kept of the meeting on the 12th of February?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: I don't know that. If there were, that would be the job of the chief's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in that context, when you say "chief," are you referring to Mr. Milosevic's office or General Ojdanic's office?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: I was referring to the chief of the General Staff, General Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And -- and who in his office would have kept minutes of this kind of meeting with President Milosevic in attendance? If you know.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: A person designated by him. If it's not recorded, it would be his chef de cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Based on your close personal experience working with General Ojdanic, would you agree with me that it seems likely this is a kind of meeting that he would have had some record made of? That would seem to be consistent with his practice from the documents we've seen and the evidence we've heard so far?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: I agree, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was there any kind of a attendance list at this meeting or -- or do you recall now, can you tell us approximately how many people attended and who they were? Besides Mr. Milosevic, yourself, and General Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Some of the officers. There was the deputy of the chief of the General Staff, General Marijanovic, and there was General Obradovic, who was the -- who was in staff affairs. General Marijanovic, as the chief's deputy. General Obradovic, as the chief of sector. The chiefs of the independent administrations. Probably the assistant for the rear. And I remember very vividly that the meeting was also attended by the commander of the 3rd Army, General Pavkovic, and the air force and anti-aircraft defence commander, General Smiljanic, and some people from the Cabinet were there, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when you say "the Cabinet," what are you referring to? Are you talking about the -- the government?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: I'm referring to the office of the chief of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And where was this meeting held?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: One of the rooms in the General Staff, but I can't say whether it was in the room where we regularly held collegium meetings or some other office. The conditions were not really very good for recording there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I'm -- I'm not sure what you mean there. "The conditions were not really very good for recording"? You mean in the room where you usually held collegium meetings? The conditions were not good for recording? You mean tape recording?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: That's what I mean, yes. In that room, microphones had been prepared and everything else. Recordings were made on a regular basis. But I don't remember in which room that particular meeting was held, because we would switch rooms depending on the purpose of the meeting and the presence of guests, for example, or who was present, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But the room where you regularly had collegium meetings was okay for recordings, apparently, because we've got lots of minutes of collegium meetings that were tape recorded. And it seems that it worked fine. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I agree. But it was very difficult to reach that office. It was two floors below ground and there was a very steep spiraling staircase. You would have to go through certain corridors and go all the way down. So maybe that's why it wasn't held there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But I took it from your earlier answer you weren't sure whether it was in the regular collegium meeting room or some other office. That's right you don't remember, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: I don't remember. I think it was not in the room where regular collegium meetings were held. That office was damaged in NATO airstrikes, so at a later date meetings could not be held there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But it was still okay on the 12th of February, 1999; right?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This -- this document, the aide-memoire, it mentions the three plans that had been drawn up, Grom 1, Grom 2, and Grom 3. What did you personally know about Grom 1 and Grom 2? Did you participate in writing either one of those?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: No. At that time, I didn't know anything, because I arrived in the General Staff only in January 1999. Later on I learnt that these plans had been drawn up considerably earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And with regard to Grom 2, this aide-memoire says that "Grom 2 is the option of engaging the Yugoslav Army in case of an armed rebellion, but only if there is insignificant involvement by the International Community." Now, I'm not sure I understand what that means. Can -- can you explain for me: If there was an armed rebellion but there was significant involvement by the International Community, then the Yugoslav Army would participate? It's not clear to me what that means.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: If we read this carefully through to the end, it says there: "Insignificant involvement of the International Community, interference by the International Community" So it -- it is to be expected. There will be no major interference by the International Community.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Interference with what? Interference with the army's involvement in dealing with the armed rebellion?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: No. First I said "the police and the army in the fight against the terrorists."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I -- I'm sorry, I didn't see that translated in your answer earlier and I didn't see it here on aide-memoire talking about Grom 2, where it says: "Grom 2 is the option of engaging the Yugoslav Army in the case of an armed rebellion." Okay. Let me move on. You say -- the document says: "This plan became outdated within only a few months." Do you know -- well, first of all, do you know when Grom 2 was first created? I know it's probably before your time on the collegium.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: I know now that that plan was drawn up in the summer of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know when it became outdated and -- and why? What happened that made it outdated?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Well, it says it became obsolete, which means that a lot of things happened from the summer of 1998 until January 1999. The Holbrooke-Milosevic Agreement was signed with Keramik [phoen] and Ivanovic. The missions arrived in Kosovo and Metohija. A number of other activities had taken place. And because of that, it was felt that this plan was now irrelevant. Another important reason is that new forces had been brought to the Mediterranean and the Adriatic, to Albania and Greece. From Greece, into Macedonia. And we had a buildup of forces on our border. So all these were new circumstances. And because of that, the plan was no longer relevant. Of course, we could not say that there would be only minor interference by the International Community as somebody who drew up this plan before my arrival had thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And another thing that happened between the summer of 1998 and January 1999 was that there had been dozens of combat operations, joint operations, with the MUP being supported by the VJ in trying to drive out the KLA in Kosovo; correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: As far as I know, the army gave support to the Ministry of the Interior to destroy terrorist groups, not to expel them from the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. That's how I see it. That's the way I view this problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. The third plan, Grom 3, is mentioned here. And it says it was drawn up after your interview in Der Spiegel -- and this means President Milosevic's interview in Der Spiegel, where you clearly stated our position. Now, does this mean that the army drew up a plan based on Mr. Milosevic's interview with the German publication Der Spiegel? That seems a strange way for the army to make its plans.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Absolutely not. No, not only because of that, but the circumstances had changed. New forces had been brought in. And there was concern that they might come in by force to save verifiers, to -- that they might be invited in to save the verifiers. I didn't read the interview. I don't know what it said. But I assume that President Milosevic said quite clear to them that he would oppose the forcible bringing of forces onto our territory without our agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That was my next question, would be whether you read it --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I believe the -- the witness used the word "inscenirana akcija," which would mean sort of a framed -- framed action, which would basically be the -- the triggering event for the -- for these forces to come in. I think this should be clarified. I am sure I heard that the witness said "inscenirana akcija."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Curcin, can you help us on -- on what's just been said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely certainly. We were afraid that NATO or the terrorists or a third party might stage-manage an action so that individual verifiers or the entire mission would appear to be under threat. And in order to rescue them, members of the multinational brigade might enter Kosovo allegedly to rescue them. That was the gist of what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you -- you told us you didn't read it, but I seem to recall from one of the collegium minutes that General Ojdanic read it and encouraged others -- or mentioned that others might want to read it as well. Do you recall that being discussed in a collegium session?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: I don't recall that. I don't know when that interview took place. If you'd help me. I can only assume that it was before the new year, before the Christmas holidays, when I was not present at the collegium.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's -- that's all right. I just wondered if you remembered, because I don't remember what date it was. Now, I'd like to go to page 3 of the English. And I'm not sure what page in B/C/S it is. It's item number 2, about what's been done by the General Staff. Do you see that? "What's been done by the General Staff in relation to the current situation"?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And -- I want to ask you about the paragraph two paragraphs above. It says: "Based on the task received, commanders of the 3rd Army and of the RV and the PVO made their decisions, which were approved at a specially organised briefing at the General Staff." And that -- that's a reference to General Pavkovic and General Smiljanic; correct? The -- the commanders of the 3rd Army and of the the -- the RV PVO. That's who those guys are.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll need you to answer out loud.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: For the record, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you recall when that specially organised briefing of the General Staff was held?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: No, I don't recall the date. I know that they came one by one, the commanders, according to our plan and invitation, to hold a briefing on the plan of use and their comments or their objections were removed, were dealt with. So that -- I assume it was in late January, but I can't recall the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Bonomy asked you a question earlier about what the collegium was, if it had a particular definition or meaning or is it a flexible or fluid organisation. And I have a follow-up question to that: In -- once -- shortly after the war started, we know there were daily evening briefings where General Ojdanic usually attended and -- and most of the generals attended, discussing the events of the day. Was there a name for those evening briefings other than "evening briefings"? Was that the collegium or was that some different group that attended the evening briefings during the wartime?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: I understand your question. It wasn't another group. Officially, we called it "analysis of the situation in the war theatre with focus on the situation in the 3rd Army and the Pristina Corps." Because in the vast majority of those evening meetings, the situation in the 3rd Army was discussed and especially in the Pristina Corps, and mostly the same persons who attended the collegium also attended these meetings. The collegium, however, was held from time to time, most often on a weekly basis, more often if needed. But in this case, we had briefings on the situation every evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm not sure that I'm clear yet. We have a briefing session on the evening of the 29th of March, 1999, and the meeting is -- is opened by General Obradovic. And -- I can give you a hard copy. I think that will help. This is actually 3D582. And General Obradovic says: "I suggest that you put your questions in accordance with the agenda. The collegium did not meet today." And then later on - I'm not sure what page it will be for you. It's page 5 of the English - it's General Ojdanic speaking. And he speaks for about the last three and a half pages. So if you can find the point where General Ojdanic starts talking, I have another sentence to read and then I have a question. Did you find that?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And General Ojdanic says: "The collegium did not meet because I was otherwise engaged." And he goes on a couple sentences later and says: "I will not be here all the time, being a member of the Supreme Command Staff." So if this is the evening briefing, and he and Obradovic are saying the collegium did not meet today, that sounds to me like the collegium is a different group that meets at a -- a different time. Now, it may be some of the same people or a lot of the same people at the evening session, but I'm trying to figure out exactly who's in the collegium and when they were meeting during the wartime. Can you help us with that?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Do you wish me to list them by name?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I -- I don't think you need to do that, because we have -- we have one collegium session from the 9th of April, 1999 during the war which lists everybody and we have collegium sessions -- we have several in late 1998 and early 1999 which list all the participants in the collegium. So I'm assuming that's the same people. But if I read this right - and you tell me if I'm wrong - if I read this right, it sounds like the collegium is meeting at a different time than these evening briefings. I see you smiling and shaking your head "no" at me. Can you explain -- can you explain what you mean?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Excuse me. You were the first to smile and you have such a winning smile, I couldn't resist smiling back.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, golly. Thanks, General.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: No, you're not correct. It's not the same. It's not the same method of working. You cannot compare the collegium of the 9th of April, where we have the list of participants, and some other collegia held in 1998. You cannot compare those with these evening briefings. These were some of the officers who were at the command post of the Supreme Command Staff. They were there all the time. They would arrive for the meetings where the situation was analysed and proposals were made to the Chief of Staff as to what should be done. And this was done every evening. It's hard for me to comment on this because there are only excerpts here. There are some sentences which are not linked together. It doesn't really make sense, because whoever was drawing up these minutes did not manage to put things down very well. So I think it creates confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Your answer you gave me just now may have helped a little bit. Could it be then when he says "the collegium didn't meet today" and he was not able to attend, there -- does that mean that there had been a scheduled meeting of the collegium on March the 29th, but it wasn't held and there wasn't another collegium meeting until the 9th of April? Would that be a fair assessment? Because that's the only other collegium meeting that we have minutes for during the war.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you elaborate?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Perhaps we should have met at 8.00. There was a time when we met at 6.00. If you noticed on the first two days, we met in the morning. So probably the Chief of Staff - most probably - had other obligations, either towards the President or somebody else, and didn't arrive on time for the beginning. He arrived later and explained that he had been away because he had other duties. But I was there, and I'm telling you that it happened the way I'm describing it. And I think it's here in the list of participants at the beginning. If you just give me another minute of your time. From the list of participants, you can see that they are not all assistants or not all the assistants are there. You can see that Colonel Ilic is there on behalf of the rear, that there are some other colonels here but not all were first assistants. They probably had other duties and tasks to perform. Some other officers are missing who usually regularly -- regularly attended. That's at the very beginning. A part of the General Staff remained in the General Staff building, a part went to the reserve command post, and some went to the rear command post. This was a time when the Supreme Command Staff was still being constituted. That's my explanation of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'm not clear yet, but let me ask another question. General Ojdanic says: I will not be here all the time being a member of the Supreme Command Staff." So where was here that he's talking about in that context? Where was the evening briefing on the 29th of March, 1999, beginning at 20.30 hours? What building were you in for this meeting?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: This evening meeting was held at the command post of the Supreme Command Staff, 124 metres below ground. Every evening there was a regular briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So are the members of the collegium also members of the Supreme Command Staff, or is the Supreme Command Staff a different group of people?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: The General Staff was in peacetime, and it was the Supreme Command Staff in wartime. Unfortunately, there is no provision in legislation governing this, but that's how we acted. That's the practice. Members of the staff who were designated as being on the command post formed the Supreme Command Staff as the most qualified staff organ to determine the use of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did the Supreme Command Staff meet in the same building as the collegium and where the evening briefings were held? Did all those take place in the same building?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: That took place at the command post of the Supreme Command Staff, not in the building, and it was always held there for the entire duration of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So all these meetings took place 124 metres below ground at the command post. Is that -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, I want to ask you about a collegium meeting on the 11th of March, 1999, and this -- I think I need to take you to page 20. We're at page 21 of the English, and it's page 19 of the B/C/S. Well -- I'm sorry. I'm sorry. Let me start at page 11 of the English. And for you, General, I think it would be -- oh, I'm sorry. This is P935. And I -- I have a hard copy, if that's easier for you, General. It will be at the bottom of what's numbered page 9 in that document you have, and in the English it's near the bottom of page 11, which has you speaking. Have you found that, General?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you're talking about some new 673 troops deployed in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, referred to the 37th Motorised Brigade relocated from the Raska garrison to Kosovska Mitrovica, and the 21st Nis Corps relocated to Urosevac. You spoke to Mr. Visnjic about that. Wasn't that in violation of the October agreements to bring those new troops into Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: First of all, regarding the page 9 at the bottom, 600-something -- 673 troops were from the reserve force, from the reserves. And you could say that it was from the peacetime composition of this brigade. I have said already that the chief of the General Staff briefly told us at that meeting of the collegium about his discussion with the general -- with General Clark and the fact that he had told him that we cannot just sit on our hands when new forces are being brought into the area. UNPREDEP had left. New forces were being brought in to replace them. And the mission was informed of this. Of course you can look at it as a violation of the agreement if you disregard the buildup of NATO forces around our borders. In my view, this cannot be viewed in isolation of everything that was going on around and that deserved our response. This is a defensive measure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But General Ojdanic himself considered it a violation, didn't he? Let's look at page 21 in the English. And for you I think it begins on page number 18. And it's in the middle of a long -- a long speech by General Ojdanic. And it's -- yeah, it's the paragraph for you that has the number 9500. Do you find that?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes. Just let me remind myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Oh. When you're ready.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General Ojdanic says --

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General Ojdanic says: "You know quite well why we had to violate. After all, what was agreed about the number of forces on the boundary and especially those that were brought in as a reinforcement to Kosovo, that has been harmonised with decisions of the President of the FRY." So General Ojdanic is acknowledging that this was a violation; correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes. If you disregard the end of that sentence, because they are building up their strength to nine and a half thousand people while we are waiting here in Belgrade for them to come in. Well, we can't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go down the -- about seven or eight lines. General Ojdanic is talking about what Clark asked him. And he said he had two main questions. "He asked me to explain to him why a 25.000-strong brigade was on the perimeter and on the Kosovo boundary." That's referring to VJ troops on the perimeters of Kosovo; correct? Isn't that what it says?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes, but that's something Clark was saying. We didn't have 25.000 in the whole territory from Kosovo to Belgrade, let alone on the boundary. That's one thing. And second, I don't think the agreement envisaged that in the vicinity of the administrative line dividing Kosovo from Serbia there should not be any forces. The closest garrison was in Raska and some other ones further in depth, like Kraljevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. But General Ojdanic goes on to say: "I said, General, because we're being threatened and we have to be able to respond adequately." So he's not saying, Wait, you're mistaken. We don't have 25.000 troops on the perimeters of Kosovo. He's saying, We have to do it because it's necessary. Isn't that -- isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Well, you can read it that way. He probably didn't want to debate with General Clark. He said what he said. But Clark knew very well that we don't have 25.000 troops in that area. No way. But General Ojdanic was probably taken aback and he didn't respond. He didn't take that up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is this an appropriate time, Your Honour? I'm sorry, General, we'll have to finish for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The problem that creates, Mr. Curcin, is that you will have to return here, and that will be on the 16th of October. And on that day, the court will be sitting at 2.15. Between now and then, it's extremely important that you do not have any discussion with anyone at all about the evidence in this case. That's the evidence we've heard or the evidence we might yet hear. You can talk about whatever you like with whoever you like as long as you keep off the subject of the evidence in this case. Now, can you please leave the courtroom with the usher and we will see you again on the 16th at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, nobody had asked me if I was able to come on that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'm afraid you will have to be here that day. I'm sorry about that. We've done our best to complete your evidence today. But obviously counsel weren't able to fit you in, so -- into the schedule and thought that your evidence merited longer. And there's nothing I -- we can do about that except require you to come back on the 16th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: General, you also developed a liking for the Prosecutor. I mean, that also brings you back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will be happy to assist you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 16th day of October 2007, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.48 p.m.,
